passage: I asked for eleven o'clock. Mummy and Papa said nine-thirty. My first reaction was a hot flush and a list of arguments ready in my throat, mostly about how Mridul's parents let him stay till midnight. But halfway through, I noticed Papa's face. The rule had been seven, and he had already moved to nine-thirty. That was a real step. So I said, "Okay, nine-thirty. Can we look at it again at Diwali?" Mummy wrote the date on the fridge calendar. Mridul thought I was mad. "Just push, they'll cave," he said. Maybe. But by December I had ten, and by February ten-thirty, each time because I had kept my word on the last one. Mridul is still fighting for midnight. I'm Saurabh, and I stopped counting it as losing.

qa.q: What hour did Mummy and Papa agree to at first?
What did Saurabh feel at the start, and what changed it?
qa.a: Saurabh felt a hot flush and an urge to argue, but noticing that Papa had already moved from seven to nine-thirty changed it into acceptance of a real step.

qa.q: What could Saurabh do if the review date brings another refusal, and why?
qa.a: Saurabh could point to the weeks of on-time returns and ask for a smaller step, because steady gains tend to expand privileges more than an all-or-nothing push.

qa.q: How might Mridul see Saurabh's choice to accept nine-thirty?
qa.a: Mridul thinks Saurabh is mad to accept less and believes pushing will make parents cave, though Mridul is still fighting for midnight.

grounding: Parents agree to an earlier hour than requested, and the teen accepts it, sets a review date and notes that gradual gains kept steadily expand privileges more than an all-or-nothing demand.

Counsellor's note, 5 December — Tanvir, Class 12
Tanvir had asked his parents to let him stay out till eleven on Saturdays. They agreed to nine. He came in today expecting me to help him "fight for the other two hours". We talked it through instead. I asked what nine gets him. He thought about it: the film, dinner with friends, the auto ride home before the roads empty. "Most of it," he admitted. We wrote a review date on his calendar, 15 January. If he keeps to nine every Saturday until then, he will ask for ten. He said, "If I fight for eleven now, I'll probably get nothing. If I keep nine for six weeks, ten is easy." He looked annoyed for about a minute, and then quite pleased with himself.
— Hafsa

qa.q: How did Tanvir seem to feel by the end?
qa.a: He looked annoyed for about a minute, then quite pleased with himself for the plan.

qa.q: Why might accepting nine lead to more freedom than fighting for eleven?
qa.a: Keeping nine steadily builds a record that makes ten an easy next step, while fighting now might lose everything.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's parents see him accepting nine?
qa.a: They may be relieved and more trusting, seeing him accept their limit calmly and plan for a fair review.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teen accepting an earlier hour than asked, setting a review date and aiming for gradual gains.

passage:
Saturday
Last night I asked Ammi and Abbu if I could go to Asif's sister's mehendi and stay till ten. They said seven-thirty. My first thought was to argue that every other girl was staying late. My second thought was the look on Abbu's face the last time I argued. So I said okay. I wrote a date on my calendar: 1 March. If I'm back by seven-thirty every time till then, I'll ask for nine. I went, I danced, I left at seven-fifteen, and Ammi raised an eyebrow when I walked in early. Maybe it's slower this way. But three months ago I wasn't allowed to go at all, and now I am. That's already more than nothing.
Urmila

qa.q: What time did Urmila get permission until?
Why did Urmila decide not to argue?
qa.a: Urmila felt tempted to argue but wary, remembering Abbu's face after the last argument, so accepting the partial yes felt wiser than risking a fight.

qa.q: Why is setting a review date useful?
qa.a: It turns the partial win into a step, with a clear chance to ask for more once Urmila has kept to the time.

qa.q: What might Ammi feel when Urmila walks in early?
qa.a: Ammi seems pleasantly surprised, raising an eyebrow, and may feel readier to trust Urmila 😊.

grounding: A teen's diary shows accepting an earlier time than asked, setting a review date and valuing steady, gradual gains.
